meta.title: Who really said "We abuse land because we regard it as a commodity belonging to us. When we see land as a community to which we belong, we may begin to use it with love and respect"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Aldo Leopold wrote it, in the Foreword to A Sand County Almanac (1949), dated 4 March 1948. Not from his essay “The Land Ethic,” as often claimed.

answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and precisely locatable. Leopold wrote it in the Foreword to A Sand County Almanac and Sketches Here and There, which he dated Madison, Wisconsin, 4 March 1948; the book was published posthumously by Oxford University Press in 1949. It is not from his essay “The Land Ethic,” where it is most often placed.

source.heading: The Foreword to A Sand County Almanac

docMeta.dd: A Sand County Almanac and Sketches Here and There

source.excerpt: Conservation is getting nowhere because it is incompatible with our Abrahamic concept of land. We abuse land because we regard it as a commodity belonging to us. When we see land as a community to which we belong, we may begin to use it with love and respect.
trail: Wikiquote’s entry for Aldo Leopold ↗ carries the sentence in its sourced section, cited to A Sand County Almanac, 1949, Foreword, p. viii — not among its disputed or misattributed lines.

We then read the Foreword itself, reproduced in full in the Aldo Leopold Foundation’s discussion guide for the book ↗. The wording matches word for word, and the Foreword closes with the signature block “Aldo Leopold / Madison, Wisconsin / 4 March 1948.”

To test the common claim that the line comes from Part III, we searched a complete text of “The Land Ethic” ↗. Neither “commodity belonging to us” nor “community to which we belong” occurs in the essay.

Leopold dated the Foreword 4 March 1948 and died 48 days later, on 21 April 1948, of a heart attack while helping neighbours fight a grass fire near Baraboo, Wisconsin, per his Wikipedia biography ↗; the book followed in 1949.
source.excerptNote: The paragraph runs on to argue that there is no other way for land to survive mechanized man; the next paragraph then splits the formulation in two, calling land-as-community the basic concept of ecology and land-as-something-loved an extension of ethics.

source.rightsNote: A Sand County Almanac and Sketches Here and There was first published in 1949 — well after the pre-1931 cut-off for US public domain — and is still in print; the Environment & Society Portal catalogue entry ↗ records the publisher as Oxford University Press and carries the notice “© by Oxford University Press.” The Aldo Leopold Foundation, established by Leopold’s five children in 1982, describes itself as the executor of his literary estate. Quoting the two sentences for identification and comment is ordinary citation; reproducing the Foreword or the book is not.

author.name: Aldo Leopold
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.metaLine: 1887–1948 · American forester, wildlife ecologist, professor of game management
author.bio: Aldo Leopold was born in Burlington, Iowa on 11 January 1887 and spent his career in forestry and wildlife science, becoming professor of game management at the University of Wisconsin in 1933 — the first professorship of its kind. He died of a heart attack on 21 April 1948 while helping neighbours fight a grass fire near his Baraboo farm, a year before the book that made his name appeared. A Sand County Almanac, assembled from his shack sketches and essays, has since sold over two million copies in ten languages and remains the founding text of the “land ethic.”

misattribution.heading: Right author, wrong chapter — and drifting words
misattribution.intro: Nobody disputes that Leopold wrote this. What goes wrong is where people say it comes from, and how the wording slips in transit.

items.why: The Sierra Club’s John Muir Exhibit page on Leopold ↗ introduces the line as coming from “Leopold’s seminal essay about the ‘land ethic’” and then runs it straight into the famous “a thing is right…” sentence from Part III with only an ellipsis between, so the two read as one passage. They are from different parts of the book: a complete text of “The Land Ethic” ↗ does not contain “commodity belonging to us” or “community to which we belong” anywhere.

items.who: “We abuse land because we see it as a commodity”
items.why: A widely liked Goodreads entry ↗ carries the sentence with “see” in place of “regard,” which flattens Leopold’s deliberate contrast between how we regard land and how we later come to see it.

items.who: “We abuse the land… see the land as a community”
items.why: Leopold wrote “land” bare, as a mass noun — the whole biotic community, not a parcel. Renderings that insert the definite article are common; a Rainwater Management feature ↗ puts that version in its headline and credits it to the 1949 book.

misattribution.truthLine: Leopold’s own words, in his own Foreword: no article before “land,” “regard” rather than “see,” and dated Madison, Wisconsin, 4 March 1948 — as the Aldo Leopold Foundation’s reproduction of the full Foreword ↗ shows.

context.heading: The last thing he wrote for the book
lead: Leopold signed the Foreword “Madison, Wisconsin, 4 March 1948.” He died 48 days later, on 21 April 1948, and the book appeared the following year. So the sentence everyone quotes is effectively his closing statement of intent — written after the essays, to tell readers what the whole collection was for.

That placement explains its shape. The Foreword is where Leopold compresses three parts of a book into a few lines of argument, and this pair of sentences is the compression: a diagnosis (land held as property) and a prescription (land held as membership). The chapter that develops the idea at length, “The Land Ethic,” sits at the far end of the book in Part III — which is very likely why so many people file the quote there.
detailsBody: Leopold wrote an earlier foreword, signed 31 July 1947, that was never used. It is longer and far more autobiographical — Arizona, predator control, the slow turn in his own thinking — and it is the source of his other most-quoted line, about living alone in a “world of wounds.” The Aldo Leopold Foundation has published an account of that discarded draft.

The 1948 replacement is shorter and structural: it walks through Parts I, II and III and then delivers the “commodity / community” formulation. Both forewords are Leopold’s; only the March 1948 one reached print in 1949.
context.pull: The book’s most-quoted sentence is not in its most-quoted chapter.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section for Aldo Leopold cites the quote to A Sand County Almanac, 1949, Foreword, p. viii, and does not list it as misattributed or disputed.

The Aldo Leopold Foundation's discussion guide reproduces the Foreword verbatim, including 'We abuse land because we regard it as a commodity belonging to us. When we see land as a community to which we belong, we may begin to use it with love and respect.', preceded by the 'Abrahamic concept of land' sentence, and ending with the signature 'Aldo Leopold / Madison, Wisconsin / 4 March 1948'. It also states the book was first published in 1949 and has sold over two million copies in ten languages, and that the foundation is the executor of Leopold's literary estate.

Aldo Leopold was born 11 January 1887 in Burlington, Iowa; died 21 April 1948 of a heart attack while helping neighbours control a grass fire near Baraboo, Wisconsin; was appointed professor of game management at the University of Wisconsin in 1933, the first such professorship.
A Sand County Almanac was published in 1949 by Oxford University Press, a year after Leopold's death, seen through the press by his son Luna.
A complete text of Leopold's essay 'The Land Ethic' does not contain the phrases 'commodity belonging to us' or 'community to which we belong'.

The Sierra Club's John Muir Exhibit page on Leopold introduces the quote as from 'Leopold's seminal essay about the "land ethic"' and joins it by ellipsis to the 'A thing is right...' sentence from Part III.
Goodreads hosts a variant reading 'We abuse land because we see it as a commodity belonging to us...' attributed to Aldo Leopold.

This Rainwater Management page headlines the quote as 'We abuse the land because we regard it as a commodity belonging to us. When we see the land as a community to which we belong...' and credits it to Aldo Leopold, author of A Sand County Almanac (1949).
The Aldo Leopold Foundation's Land Ethic page quotes 'When we see land as a community to which we belong, we may begin to use it with love and respect' and attributes it to Aldo Leopold.

The Aldo Leopold Foundation describes an unpublished 1947 foreword signed 31 July 1947, longer and more autobiographical and the source of the 'world of wounds' line, versus the shorter published foreword signed 4 March 1948.
The Environment & Society Portal entry records A Sand County Almanac and Sketches Here and There as published 1949 by Oxford University Press with the notice '© by Oxford University Press'.
